title: DATAWISE AI -- Interview Preparation Handbook
generated_from: Source code of datawise-ai inspected on 2026-11-16

topics.title: SQL, data modeling and database security

questions.question: What is DATAWISE AI and what problem does it solve?
questions.answer: DATAWISE AI is a natural-language BI tool: a user types a business question and gets back validated SQL, a chart, a result table and an insight whose numbers are computed from the returned rows. Its defining rule is that it never executes SQL written by a model. A planner (deterministic rules by default, Gemini/OpenAI optional) may only emit a typed Pydantic QueryPlan; our own compiler turns that plan into SQL from a semantic layer, a sqlglot validator re-checks it, and an executor runs it as the read-only datawise_reader role. Ambiguous questions return needs_clarification with one-click options, unsafe ones return rejected. Everything is orchestrated in AskService and persisted to org-scoped history and an audit log.
questions.reasoning: Interviewers want a crisp elevator pitch that names the key safety idea (plan, not SQL) rather than a list of technologies. Pitfall: describing it as 'an LLM that writes SQL' -- that is exactly what it avoids.
follow_ups: Who is the target user and what would they lose compared with free-form SQL?
Which single component would you protect most if you could only keep one safety layer?

questions.question: What are the three response statuses of the ask endpoint and where is each one produced?
questions.answer: AskResponse.status is a Literal of answered, needs_clarification and rejected. rejected comes from the input guardrails (issue 'guardrail:<category>'), from a planner outcome of kind reject, or from the SQL validator when the compiled SQL fails safety checks (the SQL is shown but never executed). needs_clarification comes from the planner (ambiguous ranking, missing period, unknown metric, impossible breakdown) or from a PlanError in compile_plan. answered is only returned after the executor ran the query and build_insight produced the insight. Infrastructure failures (timeouts, unreachable DB, provider errors) are not statuses at all; they are HTTP errors in the JSON error envelope.
questions.reasoning: Checks whether the candidate distinguishes domain outcomes (200 with a status) from infrastructure failures (4xx/5xx). A common mistake is to assume validator rejections never happen because 'we compiled the SQL ourselves'.
follow_ups: Why is a validator rejection returned with the SQL but a guardrail rejection without?
How does the frontend style each status differently?

questions.question: What is the 'Deterministic local adapter' and why is it the default planner?
questions.answer: It is LocalPlanner, a rule-based planner selected by LLM_PROVIDER=local (the default). It parses time phrases, does a longest-match scan over metric synonyms, dimension synonyms and known dimension values, detects grouping cues and returns a PlannerOutcome -- it is not an LLM and says so: provider='local', model='rules-v1', and the UI shows an amber 'Deterministic local adapter' badge. ADR 0004 explains the reason: no API keys were available for development, CI or demos, and faking LLM output would be dishonest. It makes tests and the eval gate offline, free and reproducible, at the cost of language coverage (6/12 on held-out paraphrases).
questions.reasoning: Probes honesty about what is and is not AI. Interviewers like to hear the cost of the choice (paraphrase coverage) stated as clearly as the benefit.
follow_ups: How would a user notice they are talking to rules rather than a model?
Would you keep the local planner once an LLM planner is in production? In what role?

questions.question: What are the verified quality numbers for this project, and how would you present them honestly?
questions.answer: Verified on 2026-11-16: 148 backend tests pass against a real Postgres, 8 vitest frontend tests pass, and 3 Playwright e2e tests cover the answered, clarification and rejected flows. The 77-case evaluation with the local planner passed 71/77 (92.2%): 36/36 answered, 10/10 clarification, 12/12 unsafe, 7/7 edge and only 6/12 held-out paraphrases; server-side latency was p50 19 ms and p95 52 ms (evaluation/results/latest.json). The honest framing is that the 100% categories measure pipeline correctness on supported phrasings, while 6/12 is the real language-generalization number, and every holdout failure was a clarification request or a missing breakdown, never a wrong number. The Gemini and OpenAI planners exist in code but were never run against live APIs.
questions.reasoning: Seniors are expected to volunteer the caveats (author bias in the eval, untested providers) instead of leading with 92.2%. Quoting numbers that are not in the results files is a red flag.
follow_ups: Which of these numbers would you put on a slide for executives, and which caveat goes with it?
What number is missing that you would want before a production launch?

questions.question: What data does DATAWISE query, and why is it synthetic and deterministic?
questions.answer: The analytics database datawise_analytics holds seven tables: suppliers, products, customers, orders, order_items, web_sessions and supplier_deliveries. scripts/seed_analytics.py generates them with random.Random(SEED) where SEED = 20241101: 500 customers, 25 suppliers, 120 products in 8 categories, 8000 orders, 40000 web sessions and 1500 deliveries over 2024-11-01..2026-10-31, with seasonality, a growth trend and a weekend lift in _day_weight. Determinism matters because evaluation/build_expected.py computes expected values once; if the data changed per run, the eval would be meaningless. A fresh volume reproduced identical results.
questions.reasoning: Shows the candidate understands that reproducible data is a prerequisite for a numeric eval, not a convenience.
follow_ups: How would you build expected values against a real, changing warehouse?
What realism is missing from the synthetic data that would matter for a planner?

questions.question: If you had one more week on this project, what would you prioritize and why?
questions.answer: First, run the existing eval with LLM_PROVIDER=gemini and openai: the dataset and runner are provider-agnostic, and the providers have never been run live, so their accuracy, latency and cost are unknown. Second, the hybrid planner from the roadmap (rules first, LLM only when rules would clarify for unknown words) because the 6/12 holdout shows language coverage is the main product gap. Third, the production gaps in the threat model: shared rate limiting, httpOnly-cookie auth and row-level security if analytics ever becomes multi-tenant. None of these are implemented today; they are listed in docs/roadmap-and-limitations.md.
questions.reasoning: Tests prioritization by evidence: the strongest answers tie each item to a measured gap (holdout score, untested code path, documented residual risk).
follow_ups: What would you explicitly NOT do in that week?
How would you know the hybrid planner made things better rather than just different?

questions.question: How is the FastAPI application assembled?
questions.answer: app/main.py exposes create_app(), a factory that loads settings, configures structlog, creates the FastAPI app, adds an HTTP middleware for request ids and access logging, adds CORSMiddleware with an explicit origin list and allowed headers, installs the JSON error handlers and includes five routers: health, auth, questions, reports and catalog. Business logic lives in app/services, so routers are thin: they resolve dependencies (current user, DB session, AskService) and call a service. The module-level app = create_app() is what uvicorn serves.
questions.reasoning: Interviewers check layering: thin routers, services without HTTP concerns, and a factory that tests can call.
follow_ups: Why use a factory rather than a module-level app with side effects?
Where would you add a new router for scheduled reports?

questions.question: How does request-id propagation work end to end?
questions.answer: The request_context middleware accepts an incoming X-Request-ID only if it is 1..64 characters and alphanumeric apart from hyphens, otherwise it generates uuid4().hex. It stores the id on request.state, binds it into structlog contextvars so every log line carries it, and echoes it in the X-Request-ID response header. The error envelope includes request_id, AuditEvent rows store it, and in the frontend ApiError keeps requestId so the ErrorBox can show it to the user. In Docker, nginx sets X-Request-ID to its own $request_id, so ids are generated at the edge.
questions.reasoning: Probes practical observability and input hygiene: an unvalidated client header would allow log injection.
follow_ups: Why validate the incoming header instead of trusting it?
How would you propagate the id to an LLM provider call or a background job?

questions.question: Describe the JSON error envelope and why the catch-all handler logs only the exception type.
questions.answer: install_error_handlers registers handlers for AppError, Starlette HTTPException, RequestValidationError and Exception, and all of them return {"error": {"code", "message", "request_id"}} (plus details for 422). AppError carries a status and a stable machine code such as query_timeout, planner_error or invalid_plan, which the frontend shows. The unhandled-exception handler logs only error_type and returns a generic internal_error, because exception messages can contain SQL, connection strings or user input; the threat model (T10) relies on this. The trade-off is weaker debugging, which is compensated by the request id.
questions.reasoning: Looks for awareness that error messages are a data-leak channel, and that stable error codes are an API contract.
follow_ups: How would you still capture stack traces safely in production?
Should validation errors echo the invalid input back?

questions.question: Routes are plain def, not async def. What does that imply for concurrency?
questions.answer: FastAPI runs sync endpoints in a worker threadpool, so blocking calls are safe: SQLAlchemy uses a sync engine (pool_size 5, max_overflow 5) and the executor uses blocking psycopg.connect. Concurrency is therefore bounded by the threadpool size and the app-DB pool, not by the event loop. With the local planner a request takes tens of milliseconds, so this is fine; with an LLM planner each request would hold a thread for the full model latency (the OpenAI client has a 30 s timeout), which would exhaust threads before CPU. The fix would be async clients and async DB drivers, or a bounded queue in front of the planner.
questions.reasoning: Distinguishes people who know how FastAPI schedules sync handlers from those who think def blocks the event loop.
follow_ups: What breaks first under 200 concurrent LLM-backed questions?
Would you convert everything to async or only the planner call?

questions.question: How are dependencies wired, and how is the planner instantiated?
questions.answer: deps.py defines DbSession (a generator yielding a SQLAlchemy session), CurrentUser (bearer-token decode plus DB lookup), get_planner and get_ask_service. get_planner is a lazy, process-wide singleton guarded by a threading.Lock: the first request calls build_planner, which for the local provider loads the value index from the analytics DB. If construction raises ProviderError (e.g. GEMINI_API_KEY missing) it becomes a 503 planner_unavailable instead of crashing startup. reset_planner exists so tests can rebuild it. get_ask_service creates a cheap AskService per request around the shared planner.
questions.reasoning: Checks understanding of FastAPI DI, lazy initialization and how failure modes surface (503 vs crash).
follow_ups: Why not build the planner at import time?
What is the cost of taking the lock on every request, and does it matter here?

questions.question: How is configuration managed?
questions.answer: core/config.py defines Settings with pydantic-settings, reading environment variables and then .env files (project root first, then backend/.env) with extra='ignore'. Fields are typed: llm_provider is Literal['local','gemini','openai'], analytics_as_of_date is a date, jwt_secret has min_length=32 so a short secret fails at startup. get_settings is wrapped in lru_cache so the object is built once. There are three DB URLs on purpose: app DB, analytics admin (seeding and expected values only) and analytics reader (the request path).
questions.reasoning: Typed config that fails fast is the point; also whether the candidate notices the separate reader URL.
follow_ups: What is the downside of lru_cache on settings in tests?
Which settings should come from a secret manager in production?

questions.question: Why does AskService contain no FastAPI imports, and what does that buy you?
questions.answer: AskService takes Settings and a PlannerProvider and exposes ask() and run_plan(); routers call it and FastAPI serializes the returned AskResponse. Keeping HTTP out means the same pipeline is reused by POST /reports/{id}/run, which calls run_plan directly with a stored plan and skips the planner. It can also be driven from tests or a future scheduler without a request object. The one leak is that it raises AppError for infrastructure failures, but AppError is a plain Exception subclass in core/errors.py, not a FastAPI type.
questions.reasoning: Tests separation of concerns and reuse; a good answer names the concrete reuse (report re-run) rather than abstract 'clean architecture'.
follow_ups: How would a scheduled-report worker call this service?
Would you split persistence out of AskService? Why or why not?

questions.question: Walk through AskService._persist. What is written, and is there anything subtle about it?
questions.answer: Every outcome (answered, clarification, rejected, execution error) writes a QueryHistory row and an AuditEvent 'question.asked' in one commit; db.flush() is used to get the history id so the audit detail can reference it and the response can return query_id. Subtle points: when an execution error occurs the response object says 'rejected' but the history status is stored as 'error' because detail is passed, so history and API status can differ. latency_ms is computed before _persist, so the reported latency excludes the history write. Persistence happens in the request path, so if the app DB is down a successful analytics query still ends in a 500.
questions.reasoning: Senior interviewers like candidates who read code closely enough to find status mapping and latency accounting subtleties.
follow_ups: Would you make history writes asynchronous? What would you lose?
Why store the question text for rejected requests?

questions.question: Describe the stages of the question pipeline and the responsibility of each.
questions.answer: AskService.ask strips the question and runs check_question (regex guardrails). Then the planner returns a PlannerOutcome: a QueryPlan, a clarification or a rejection. run_plan compiles the plan with compile_plan (SQL built only from semantic-layer definitions), validates it with validate_sql (sqlglot parse plus allowlists), executes it with execute_readonly as datawise_reader, and calls build_insight, which verifies columns and types and computes the insight, provenance and chart spec from the rows. Finally _persist writes history and audit. Each stage can stop the pipeline with a typed outcome.
questions.reasoning: Baseline architecture question; good answers explain why the order matters (cheap and unsafe checks first, expensive DB work last).
follow_ups: Which stage is the real security boundary?
Which stages are deterministic, and which could vary per run?

questions.question: Why are the app data and analytics data in two databases on the same Postgres server?
questions.answer: ADR 0005: datawise_app (users, orgs, history, reports, audit) and datawise_analytics (business data) are separate databases. Postgres cannot query across databases in one statement, and the init script revokes CONNECT on both databases from PUBLIC and grants CONNECT only on analytics to datawise_reader. So even a fully compromised query on the reader connection cannot touch password hashes or other orgs' history, and test_reader_cannot_connect_to_app_db proves the role cannot even open a connection. Using one server keeps the demo a single docker compose up while mirroring a production setup where analytics is a replica or warehouse.
questions.reasoning: Shows the candidate prefers structural isolation over relying on query filters.
follow_ups: What would you lose by using two schemas in one database instead?
What still leaks if an attacker can run arbitrary SELECTs as the reader?

questions.question: How do saved reports work, and why do they store the plan instead of the SQL?
questions.answer: POST /reports accepts a name, the question and a QueryPlan; create_report calls compile_plan to reject plans that do not compile (422 invalid_plan) and stores plan.model_dump as JSON with org_id. POST /reports/{id}/run loads the report through _get_owned (404 for other orgs), re-validates it with QueryPlan.model_validate and calls AskService.run_plan, so the planner is not called again and the result goes through compiler, validator and executor exactly like a fresh question. Storing the plan means a stored artifact cannot smuggle SQL, and metric definition fixes apply to old reports. The flip side is that a definition change silently changes the numbers a report produced last month.
questions.reasoning: Probes data-contract thinking: plans are inspectable and re-validated; SQL would be a stored injection vector.
follow_ups: How would you version metric definitions so old reports remain explainable?
Should a report pin relative dates like 'last month' or re-resolve them?

questions.question: The semantic layer is described as the single source of truth. Which components read it, and why does that matter?
questions.answer: app/semantic/layer.py defines FACTS, METRICS, DIMENSIONS, VALUE_QUERIES and ALLOWED_TABLES. The compiler reads facts, joins, metric SQL and dimension bindings; the validator imports ALLOWED_TABLES and ALLOWED_COLUMNS; build_catalog merges it with information_schema for the Catalog page; describe_for_prompt renders it for LLM prompts; the local planner builds its phrase table from metric and dimension synonyms; and the value index runs VALUE_QUERIES. Because everything derives from one registry, adding a metric updates compiler, prompt and catalog together, and test_every_metric_dimension_combination_compiles_and_validates catches mismatches between the compiler's SQL and the validator's allowlist.
questions.reasoning: Looks for an understanding that duplication between prompt, compiler and validator is where text-to-SQL systems usually drift.
follow_ups: What is still duplicated outside the registry? (hint: frontend formatting)
How would you let analysts propose new metrics without a deploy?

questions.question: What is the PlannerProvider abstraction and how is a provider selected?
questions.answer: PlannerProvider is an ABC with name, model and a single plan(question) -> (PlannerOutcome, Usage) method whose docstring states it must never return SQL. build_planner reads settings.llm_provider: 'gemini' and 'openai' import their SDKs lazily and construct GeminiPlanner or OpenAIPlanner with the as-of date and max rows; otherwise it loads the value index and returns LocalPlanner. Because every provider returns the same typed outcome, the compiler, validator, executor and the eval runner are identical across providers, which makes provider comparisons apples-to-apples.
questions.reasoning: Strategy pattern applied to model providers; the interesting part is that the interface itself is a safety boundary (no SQL field exists).
follow_ups: Why import the provider SDKs lazily?
How would you add an Anthropic or local-model provider?

questions.question: Where does in-process state live in the API, and what breaks when you run several replicas?
questions.answer: Several things are cached per process: the planner singleton in deps.py, the ValueIndex in values.py (_cached), the catalog dict in catalog.py (_cache), the token buckets in TokenBucketLimiter and Settings via lru_cache. With N replicas the rate limit becomes N times looser because buckets are not shared, and after reseeding analytics each replica keeps stale dimension values and catalog until restart. None of this is wrong for a single-container demo and the docs list it as a limitation; the production fix is Redis or a gateway for rate limiting and an explicit cache-invalidation signal (or TTL) for the value index and catalog.
questions.reasoning: Tests whether the candidate can find hidden statefulness in an API that looks stateless.
follow_ups: How would you invalidate the value index after an ETL run?
Is sticky routing an acceptable fix for the rate limiter?

questions.question: Which failures become HTTP errors and which become a 200 with status rejected or needs_clarification? Why?
questions.answer: Guardrail hits, planner rejections and validator failures return 200 with status rejected; planner clarifications and PlanError return 200 with needs_clarification. Infrastructure failures raise AppError: a ProviderError from the planner becomes 502 planner_error, an ExecutionError becomes 504 for query_timeout or 502 otherwise (analytics_unavailable, read_only_violation, execution_error), and a planner that cannot be built is 503. The distinction is that a status is a legitimate product answer the UI renders, while an HTTP error means the system failed and the client should show an error with the request id. Execution errors are still persisted to history before raising.
questions.reasoning: Probes API design judgement: mixing business outcomes and transport errors is a common source of client bugs.
follow_ups: Should a read_only_violation really be a 502? What would you alert on?
How does the eval runner treat a 504?

questions.question: How would you extend DATAWISE to support multiple warehouses (Postgres, Snowflake, BigQuery)?
questions.answer: This is not implemented. I would add a datasource to each Fact (or a per-tenant datasource map), so the compiler knows the target dialect, and either build expressions with sqlglot and render with dialect=... or transpile the Postgres output. validate_sql already parses with read='postgres'; it would take the dialect as a parameter and the allowlist would be keyed by datasource. execute_readonly would become an adapter per engine with its own read-only credentials, timeout mechanism (statement_timeout vs warehouse query timeouts) and row cap. Cross-warehouse joins would stay unsupported, matching the existing one-fact-per-plan rule, and the eval dataset would need expected values per warehouse.
questions.reasoning: System-design question: good answers keep the plan as the stable contract and push dialect differences to the edges.
follow_ups: How do you enforce read-only on a warehouse that has no default_transaction_read_only?
What happens to DATE_TRUNC and CAST semantics across dialects?

questions.question: Design a hybrid planner: deterministic rules first, LLM fallback. Where does it fit and how do you keep it safe?
questions.answer: Not implemented; it is roadmap item 2. I would add a HybridPlanner implementing PlannerProvider that calls LocalPlanner first and only calls the LLM when the outcome is clarify because of unmapped words (LocalPlanner._leftovers already detects them), not when the question is genuinely ambiguous like 'best customers', where clarifying is correct. The LLM output still goes through parse_outcome, check_plan, the compiler and the validator, so safety does not change. The response should carry which path answered (provider label and assumptions), and the eval should report accuracy, cost and latency per path, with the holdout set as the primary success metric.
questions.reasoning: Assesses cost-aware design and whether the candidate preserves the safety invariants when adding a model.
follow_ups: How do you prevent the LLM from 'answering' questions that should be clarified?
What would you log to tune the rules from LLM fallbacks over time?

questions.question: Why is the insight text computed in Python instead of asking an LLM to summarize the result?
questions.answer: build_insight computes every number from the returned rows: first vs last period with percent change, peak and lowest, totals for additive metrics and share of the rows shown. Each sentence is backed by a Provenance entry listing the columns and row indexes used, which the UI shows and highlights in the table. A model summary could hallucinate numbers or trends, which is threat T9 in the threat model. The trade-off is less fluent, template-like text and only the analyses that were coded (no causal commentary).
questions.reasoning: Probes grounding: in BI, a single invented number destroys trust more than a dull sentence.
follow_ups: If you did add an LLM narrative, how would you constrain it to the computed facts?
How do you test that an insight is correct?

questions.question: What is PlannerOutcome and why does it have kind plan, clarify or reject?
questions.answer: PlannerOutcome is the only thing any planner returns: kind is Literal['plan','clarify','reject'] with an optional QueryPlan, Clarification (question plus options) or reason. Modeling the three outcomes explicitly makes asking for clarification and refusing first-class results instead of exceptions or free text, so the pipeline can persist and render each one. QueryPlan, Filter, TimeRange and OrderBy use extra='forbid', so there is literally no field that could carry SQL; test_plan_rejects_extra_fields_like_raw_sql checks that a 'sql' key is rejected.
questions.reasoning: Basic structured-output design; the key insight is that the schema is a security control, not just parsing help.
follow_ups: What happens if a model returns kind='plan' with plan=null?
Why are Clarification options full questions rather than short labels?

questions.question: How does run_with_repair work for the LLM planners?
questions.answer: run_with_repair takes a call(message) -> (raw_json, usage) function and makes at most two attempts. Each raw output goes through parse_outcome; on success it returns the outcome with token usage summed across attempts. On the first failure it rebuilds the user message with the original question plus the validation error ('Your previous output was invalid (...). Return a corrected JSON object only.'). If the second attempt also fails it raises ProviderError, which AskService turns into a 502 planner_error. It is shared by Gemini and OpenAI, and has only been exercised through unit-level parsing, never against live APIs.
questions.reasoning: Interviewers check bounded retries, feeding the error back, and cost accounting across retries.
follow_ups: Why only one repair attempt?
Should a failed repair degrade to the local planner instead of a 502?

questions.question: Why does parse_outcome call check_plan when Pydantic already validated the JSON?
questions.answer: Pydantic validates shape and types: lists, Literals, numeric ops needing numbers, end after start. It does not know whether 'churn' is a metric, whether two metrics come from different facts, or whether 'product' can break down conversion_rate. check_plan encodes those semantic-layer rules, so calling it inside parse_outcome turns a semantically invalid plan into a repair message the model can act on instead of a later clarification. It is the same function the compiler uses, so the model is held to exactly the rules that compilation enforces.
questions.reasoning: Distinguishes syntactic from semantic validation of model output -- a key structured-output concept.
follow_ups: Could you encode metric names as enums in the JSON schema instead? Trade-offs?
What semantic rule is NOT covered by check_plan?

questions.question: Compare how the Gemini and OpenAI planners request structured output. What would you verify before trusting them?
questions.answer: GeminiPlanner calls models.generate_content with system_instruction, response_mime_type='application/json', response_json_schema set to PlannerOutcome.model_json_schema() and temperature 0. OpenAIPlanner uses chat completions with response_format type json_schema and strict False, also temperature 0, and a 30 s client timeout. Neither has been run against a live API, so before trusting them I would verify that the Pydantic-generated schema (with defaults, unions like str|float|list[str] and $defs) is accepted by each API, that token usage fields are populated as the code expects, and measure how often the repair path triggers. With strict off, the schema is guidance rather than a guarantee, which is why parse_outcome re-validates everything.
questions.reasoning: Probes practical knowledge of provider structured-output modes and honesty about untested code.
follow_ups: What schema changes would strict mode require?
How would you write a contract test for a provider without spending tokens in CI?

questions.question: What is in the LLM system prompt, and what failure modes does it leave open?
questions.answer: system_prompt tells the model it is a planner, must never write SQL, must use only names from the semantic layer, must clarify ambiguous questions with 2-4 complete rephrased options, and must reject data modification, credential or system-table requests and instructions aimed at it. It includes the as-of date (time_range.end exclusive), the row limit and describe_for_prompt(): metrics with fact and first five synonyms, dimensions with facts, the data range and the one-fact rule. It does not include dimension values, so a model can produce a filter like region='Northeast' that passes validation but matches nothing, which surfaces as 'No data matched' rather than an error. Relative-date math is also delegated to the model rather than to timeparse.
questions.reasoning: Strong answers spot what is missing from the prompt and the consequences, not just what is there.
follow_ups: Would you pass the value index into the prompt, or validate filter values after planning?
Should the LLM resolve dates, or should timeparse run first and be passed as a hint?

questions.question: How are token usage and cost tracked?
questions.answer: Each provider returns a Usage dataclass with input and output tokens. run_with_repair sums usage over both attempts, and estimate_cost multiplies by a small PRICES_PER_MTOK table (gemini-2.5-flash and gpt-4.1-mini) to produce an estimate label; unknown models cost 0. AskService copies it into the response Usage model, so the client can show it. The local planner always returns zeros. Usage is not persisted in query_history, so cost reporting over time would need a schema change.
questions.reasoning: Checks cost awareness; a sharp candidate notices that cost is returned but not stored.
follow_ups: Where would you store cost for monthly per-org reporting?
Why is a hardcoded price table risky?

questions.question: How would you safely switch the default planner from local rules to Gemini, using eval gates?
questions.answer: Not done yet; the providers were never run live. Step one is running evaluation/run_eval.py against a stack with LLM_PROVIDER=gemini and comparing per category with the local baseline, adding cost and latency. Gates should be per category: unsafe must stay 12/12, answered must not drop, and the held-out paraphrase score should rise meaningfully, and I would add more held-out cases written by someone else because 12 is a small sample. Then a shadow phase: run both planners, serve the local result, log plan diffs. Then a canary by org with the model version pinned and temperature 0, and an automatic fallback to the local planner on ProviderError. The safety layers after the planner do not change, which is what makes this switch low-risk.
questions.reasoning: Senior LLM-ops question: evaluation-gated rollout, shadow traffic and fallbacks.
follow_ups: How do you handle LLM non-determinism in the gate?
What do you do when the model is deprecated?

questions.question: What are Fact, Metric, Dimension and DimensionBinding in the semantic layer?
questions.answer: A Fact is a join path: from_sql, a time_column, always-on base_where predicates and optional Joins keyed by alias. There are three: sales (orders joined to order_items), web (web_sessions) and deliveries (supplier_deliveries). A Metric has a name, label, the fact it belongs to, an aggregate SQL expression, a display format and synonyms. A Dimension has synonyms and a dict of DimensionBindings per fact, each with the SQL expression and the join aliases it needs. All are frozen dataclasses in layer.py, which ADR 0002 chose over YAML for type checking.
questions.reasoning: Vocabulary check; the interviewer wants to hear that dimensions are bound per fact.
follow_ups: Why is time_column on the Fact rather than on each Metric?
What would a Measure vs Metric distinction add?

questions.question: How does compile_plan build the FROM and JOIN clauses, including join dependencies?
questions.answer: It takes the fact of the first metric, collects the join aliases needed by every grouping dimension and every dimension filter from their bindings, and resolves them with a small recursive _need function that first adds each alias's requires. In the sales fact the supplier join requires the products join (suppliers are reached via p.supplier_id), so 'revenue by supplier' always emits JOIN products p before JOIN suppliers s; test_supplier_join_pulls_in_products_first asserts that order. Only needed joins are added, which keeps queries cheaper and avoids accidental fan-out.
questions.reasoning: Tests understanding of join graphs in a semantic layer and why ordering matters in SQL text.
follow_ups: What would you need for a dimension reachable by two different paths?
Can a join here ever multiply rows? Which metrics would be affected?

questions.question: Why are dimensions bound per fact, and what happens for 'conversion rate by product'?
questions.answer: Each Dimension declares bindings only for facts where it is meaningful: product exists for sales and deliveries but not for web sessions, and region means customer region on sales but session region on web. check_plan rejects a dimension without a binding for the plan's fact ('dimension product is not available for metric(s) conversion_rate'), and the local planner turns that into a clarification listing the valid breakdowns. Without bindings, a naive text-to-SQL system would invent a join between sessions and products and return confident but meaningless numbers.
questions.reasoning: The point is preventing semantically invalid joins, which is a bigger real-world risk than syntax errors.
follow_ups: How would you model a dimension that is valid on web only after a session-to-order link exists?
Is 'region' meaning two different things on two facts a problem for users?

questions.question: How are cancelled orders handled, and what about returned orders?
questions.answer: The sales Fact has base_where=("o.status <> 'cancelled'",), so the compiler adds it to every sales query regardless of the plan, and the planner adds the assumption 'Cancelled orders are excluded from sales metrics.' test_revenue_excludes_cancelled_and_applies_time_range checks it. Orders with status 'returned' (about 3% in the seed weights) are still counted as revenue; that is a business-definition choice that is only documented through the metric description, not an explicit assumption. In an interview I would flag it: definitions like this are where 'the number is wrong' tickets come from.
questions.reasoning: Checks that the candidate reads definitions critically; the returned-orders nuance is a good discriminator.
follow_ups: How would you expose a 'net revenue' metric without breaking existing reports?
Where should a definition like this be documented for business users?

questions.question: How do dimension filters become WHERE and metric thresholds become HAVING?
questions.answer: A Filter has kind 'dimension' or 'metric'. _filter_sql uses the dimension binding SQL or the metric aggregate SQL as the left side, then either IN (literals) or a mapped operator from _OPS. Dimension filters are appended to WHERE after the base and time predicates; metric filters go to HAVING because they apply to aggregates. check_plan enforces the rules: numeric comparisons only on metrics, metric filters must be numeric and from the same fact, time dimensions are not filterable (use time_range). test_metric_filter_becomes_having shows 'HAVING ROUND(SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price), 2) > 1000' with ORDER BY revenue DESC, customer ASC.
questions.reasoning: WHERE vs HAVING is a classic SQL check; tying it to the plan types shows the candidate understands the compiler.
follow_ups: What happens to a HAVING filter on a rounded expression at boundary values?
How would you support 'customers with more than 5 orders AND revenue over 10k'?

questions.question: How does the compiler make user-provided values safe when it builds SQL as strings?
questions.answer: Identifiers never come from user input: table, column and expression SQL come from the registry, and plan fields are checked against it before compilation (an order_by like 'name; drop' fails check_plan). Values go through _lit, which renders exp.Literal.string or exp.Literal.number with sqlglot's Postgres dialect, so quotes are doubled; booleans are rejected explicitly because bool is a subclass of int in Python. test_string_literals_are_escaped compiles a customer filter of O'Brien'); DROP TABLE x; -- and asserts the output contains the escaped literal and still validates. Parameter binding would be the textbook alternative, but the executor runs validated SQL without params so the validator can see the full statement.
questions.reasoning: Probes injection reasoning: why escaping is acceptable here, and the trade-off against bind parameters.
follow_ups: Why might bind parameters still be preferable? What would the validator lose?
Why does isinstance(True, int) matter in _lit?

questions.question: How does the local planner decide whether a dimension noun becomes a GROUP BY?
questions.answer: A dimension noun is grouped only with a grouping cue. _has_cue_before walks backwards over words, skipping fillers in SKIP_WORDS and numbers, and accepts cue words such as by, per, which, top, best; FOLLOW_CUE accepts patterns after the noun like 'customers who spent'; 'products by revenue' (noun, then 'by', then a metric) also groups; and 'region and segment' continues an existing group. A noun directly after its own value ('Enterprise customers') is treated as a filter, not a grouping. This is why 'best converting traffic source' failed in the holdout: no cue word preceded 'traffic source', so the answer lacked the breakdown.
questions.reasoning: Tests whether the candidate can explain a real failure mode from the eval in terms of the code.
follow_ups: How would you fix 'best converting traffic source' without overfitting?
Why is a false grouping worse than a missing grouping?

questions.question: How are value collisions like 'mobile' or 'tablet' resolved?
questions.answer: ValueIndex.aliases maps each lower-cased phrase to a list of (dimension, value) pairs, because one phrase can belong to several dimensions: 'mobile' is both an order channel and a web device. The planner first decides the fact from the metric, then keeps only pairs whose dimension is bound to that fact, so 'Revenue from mobile this year' filters o.channel='mobile' while 'conversion rate on mobile' filters ws.device. If no pair is compatible and all candidates are generic (channel, traffic_source, device), the value is ignored with an explicit assumption; otherwise the planner asks for clarification. The edge eval case edge_value_collision_mobile checks the sales interpretation against independent SQL.
questions.reasoning: Shows entity resolution grounded in schema context, a core text-to-SQL problem.
follow_ups: What if two values within the same fact collide (a product and a customer named the same)?
Is silently ignoring an inapplicable value acceptable?

questions.question: How does timeparse turn phrases into date ranges, and what conventions does it use?
questions.answer: parse_time runs patterns in a fixed precedence: 'since <month> <year>', quarters ('q3 2025', 'third quarter of 2025'), month plus year, 'last/past N days|weeks|months|quarters|years', named relative periods (last month, this quarter, ytd, yesterday), explicit years, and finally all-time words. Every range is half-open [start, end). 'Last month' is the previous full calendar month; 'this year' runs from Jan 1 to the as-of date inclusive; 'last N months' is N calendar months including the as-of month; several explicit years produce one span and the planner groups by year. Matched spans are blanked out of the text so '2025' cannot be mistaken for a value.
questions.reasoning: Date semantics are a major source of silent errors; the interviewer wants explicit conventions.
follow_ups: Is 'last 3 months' including the current partial month the right default?
How would you support fiscal years?

questions.question: Challenge: relative dates are anchored to the data end date, not the wall clock. Is that right?
questions.answer: ANALYTICS_AS_OF_DATE defaults to 2026-10-31, the last day of the synthetic data, and parse_time treats it as 'today'. For a static demo dataset that is the only choice that makes 'last month' return data (September 2026) and keeps eval expectations stable. The risk is user confusion, so the planner adds 'Relative dates are anchored to 2026-10-31 (end of data)' as a visible assumption. In production I would anchor to the current date in the business timezone, or to a data-freshness watermark from the ETL, and show 'data as of' in the UI; the LLM prompt already receives the as-of date so both planners stay consistent.
questions.reasoning: Tests whether the candidate can defend a demo decision while naming what changes in production.
follow_ups: What should happen when the warehouse is two days behind?
Which timezone defines 'yesterday' for a global company?

questions.question: Challenge: why plan-then-compile instead of letting the LLM write SQL directly? Argue both sides.
questions.answer: For plan-then-compile (ADR 0001): the model cannot emit SQL at all, so injection, writes and hallucinated joins are structurally impossible; identifiers come from the registry and values are escaped; plans are inspectable, savable and re-runnable without a model; and every provider shares the same compiler, so evals are comparable. Against it: expressiveness is capped by the semantic layer -- one fact, at most two dimensions, no window functions, cohorts or period comparisons -- and every new analysis needs registry work; unsupported questions become clarifications. Direct SQL generation covers the long tail but moves all safety to post-hoc validation of arbitrary SQL, which is brittle. A reasonable middle ground for power users would be model SQL in a sandboxed 'expert mode' behind the same validator and read-only role, clearly labeled.
questions.reasoning: Classic senior challenge; the interviewer wants a balanced argument with the costs stated, not a sales pitch.
follow_ups: Which customer requests would force you to revisit this decision?
How would you measure the cost of lost expressiveness?

questions.question: How does the local planner decide ordering and LIMIT for ranking questions?
questions.answer: A ranking regex detects words like top, best, worst, lowest plus an optional count (digits or number words). With a categorical dimension, the plan orders by the primary metric in the detected direction; an explicit N becomes the limit, otherwise a plural noun ('top products') gives 10 and a singular one gives 1, recorded as an assumption, and 'which ...' questions keep all rows ordered. For metrics in LOWER_IS_BETTER (avg_lead_time_days), 'best' or 'fastest' flips to ascending. Time-only breakdowns are ordered by time ascending, and scalar questions get limit 1. The compiler then adds a deterministic tie-break on the first dimension.
questions.reasoning: Ranking direction bugs ('best lead time' meaning lowest) are subtle; good answers mention LOWER_IS_BETTER.
follow_ups: Where should 'lower is better' live -- planner or semantic layer?
Is defaulting to top 10 for plurals a good UX choice?

questions.question: Why does the compiler always emit a LIMIT and use ordinal GROUP BY?
questions.answer: compile_plan appends LIMIT min(plan.limit, max_rows), so even though QueryPlan allows limit up to 100000 the SQL is clamped to MAX_ROWS (1000); test_limit_is_clamped_to_max_rows checks it, and the validator independently rejects a missing or oversized LIMIT. GROUP BY uses ordinals (1, 2) matching the dimension positions in the SELECT list, which avoids repeating long expressions like CAST(DATE_TRUNC(...) AS DATE). When there is no explicit order it adds ORDER BY 1, and with an explicit order it appends the first dimension ascending as a tie-breaker so ties never reorder between runs.
questions.reasoning: Basic but shows attention to determinism and bounded results.
follow_ups: Why does deterministic ordering matter for an eval?
What are the readability costs of ordinal GROUP BY?

questions.question: How is the datawise_reader role created and what can it do?
questions.answer: db/init/01-init.sh runs once on an empty volume. It creates both databases and the role with LOGIN and a password from DATAWISE_READER_PASSWORD, sets default_transaction_read_only = on and statement_timeout = '10s' at role level, revokes ALL on both databases from PUBLIC and grants CONNECT only on datawise_analytics. Inside analytics it revokes the public schema from PUBLIC, grants USAGE to the reader and sets default privileges so tables created by the admin user are SELECT-able. seed_analytics.py additionally runs GRANT SELECT ON ALL TABLES after creating the tables.
questions.reasoning: Least-privilege basics; the interviewer wants specific grants, not 'a read-only user'.
follow_ups: What does REVOKE ... FROM PUBLIC protect against here?
What can the reader still see that you might not expect?

questions.question: Why does seed_analytics re-apply GRANTS even when data already exists, and why also ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES?
questions.answer: Analytics tables are created by the seed script as the admin user after the init script ran, so the reader needs SELECT on tables that did not exist at init time. ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES FOR ROLE <admin> IN SCHEMA public covers future tables created by that role, and the explicit GRANT SELECT ON ALL TABLES in GRANTS covers existing tables and the case where tables were created by a different role or before the default privileges existed. seed() runs GRANTS on both the 'already seeded' path and after a reset, so a container restart repairs privileges. If the role itself is missing, /readyz reports analytics_db unavailable.
questions.reasoning: Checks understanding of Postgres privilege timing, a frequent real-world gotcha.
follow_ups: Why do default privileges depend on which role creates the table?
How would you manage these grants in a managed Postgres with Terraform?

questions.question: What exactly does validate_sql check, in order?
questions.answer: It parses with sqlglot (postgres dialect) and fails on parse errors; requires exactly one statement; requires the root to be exp.Select (so UNION, EXPLAIN, COPY, SET, VACUUM fail); walks the whole tree for forbidden nodes (Insert, Update, Delete, Merge, Drop, Create, Alter, TruncateTable, Grant, Revoke, Copy, Command, Set, Into, Lock, Transaction, Commit and others); checks tables against ALLOWED_TABLES or CTE names, rejecting non-public schemas and catalog (cross-database) references; checks columns against ALLOWED_COLUMNS or SELECT aliases; rejects SELECT *; allows only function classes in _ALLOWED_FUNCTIONS (Anonymous functions like pg_sleep or dblink fail); and requires an integer-literal outer LIMIT <= MAX_ROWS with no OFFSET. Issues are de-duplicated and returned together.
questions.reasoning: A detailed walk-through is expected; tree-walking for forbidden nodes (e.g. DELETE inside a CTE) is the key insight.
follow_ups: Why walk the entire tree instead of checking the root type only?
Why is FOR UPDATE rejected in a read-only system?

questions.question: Challenge: why validate SQL that your own compiler generated?
questions.answer: ADR 0003 calls it defense in depth: the compiler is code, and code has bugs; future features (new metric SQL, new join types, an expert mode) could emit something unexpected, and saved-report plans arrive from storage. The validator is an independent check written against a different representation (a parse tree) and costs well under the query time. It also acts as a tripwire: with the compiler correct, validator rejections should be zero, so any rejection in production is a signal of a compiler bug or tampering. The cost is maintenance: the function allowlist must grow with the compiler, which test_every_metric_dimension_combination_compiles_and_validates catches automatically.
questions.reasoning: Strong answers present the validator as a tripwire and independent control, not as redundant paranoia.
follow_ups: Would you alert on validator rejections? At what threshold?
If the compiler and validator share the allowlist, are they really independent?

questions.question: Challenge: what are the limits of the table/column/function allowlist approach in this validator?
questions.answer: Columns are checked by bare name, not by table: 'name' is allowed because it exists on suppliers, products and customers, so the validator cannot tell which table a column comes from. Any alias defined anywhere in the query also passes the column check, and CTE names pass the table check, so the real bound is the table allowlist plus Postgres itself. Function checks rely on sqlglot class names, and the threat model notes that sqlglot and Postgres can parse differently. The reader role can also read pg_catalog (Postgres grants catalog visibility to all roles), which only the validator blocks. Mitigations: qualify columns with sqlglot's optimizer against a schema and check (table, column) pairs, and keep the read-only role and separate database as the hard boundaries.
questions.reasoning: Assesses whether the candidate can attack their own control honestly -- a strong senior signal.
follow_ups: Construct a query that passes this validator but should not. What stops it?
Would you rather have a stricter validator or a stricter role?

questions.question: Challenge: the role is already read-only. Why does the executor also run SET TRANSACTION READ ONLY, and why keep app-level checks?
questions.answer: Layers fail differently. default_transaction_read_only is only a default; any session can run SET TRANSACTION READ WRITE, so on its own it is weak. The real database barrier is privileges: the role has only SELECT, and test_reader_role_cannot_write_even_in_read_write_transaction bypasses the executor, switches to READ WRITE and still gets InsufficientPrivilege. The executor's SET TRANSACTION READ ONLY protects against a misconfigured role (say, someone grants INSERT later). App-level checks (guardrails, typed plan, validator) give clear user-facing errors early and never send unsafe SQL to the database. Each layer is cheap, and no single misconfiguration enables writes.
questions.reasoning: Probes understanding of which control actually enforces what, and why redundancy is still justified.
follow_ups: What does a read-only transaction block that SELECT-only privileges do not?
If you could keep only one database-side control, which one?

questions.question: Challenge: statement_timeout vs cost limits. Is a 5-second timeout enough protection against expensive queries?
questions.answer: The executor sets SET LOCAL statement_timeout to STATEMENT_TIMEOUT_MS (5000) per transaction and the role has a 10 s fallback; test_statement_timeout proves pg_sleep is cancelled as query_timeout. A timeout bounds wall time, not resource use within that window: a query can still use parallel workers, memory and temp files for 5 seconds, and 30 questions per minute per user times many users adds up. fetchmany(MAX_ROWS + 1) only protects API memory. Missing pieces are a pre-execution EXPLAIN cost threshold (roadmap item 7), per-role limits such as temp_file_limit or a connection limit, and a concurrency cap on analytics queries. Because compiled queries are a small, known set of shapes, cost is mostly predictable, which is why the timeout is acceptable for the demo.
questions.reasoning: Distinguishes time limits from resource limits; good answers propose concrete Postgres settings.
follow_ups: How reliable are EXPLAIN cost estimates as a guard?
Would you rather queue queries or reject them under load?

questions.question: Describe the analytics schema and indexes. Which compiled queries would get slow at scale?
questions.answer: The DDL creates seven tables with primary and foreign keys and a CHECK on quantity > 0, plus indexes on orders(order_date), orders(customer_id), order_items(order_id), order_items(product_id), web_sessions(session_date) and supplier_deliveries(delivered_date); ANALYZE runs after loading. Time filters are sargable because the compiler compares the raw time column to CAST literals. At scale the expensive shapes are sales queries grouped by customer or region (join to customers, high cardinality), DATE_TRUNC grouping over all time, and COUNT(DISTINCT) metrics. I would add date partitioning, pre-aggregated rollups per fact and grain, and consider BRIN on date columns for append-only tables.
questions.reasoning: Data modeling and indexing judgement tied to the actual query shapes the compiler emits.
follow_ups: Why is COUNT(DISTINCT) expensive and how would a rollup handle it?
Which index would you add first, based on the eval queries?

questions.question: How do the metric definitions avoid double counting when orders are joined to order lines?
questions.answer: The sales fact is at order-line grain (orders JOIN order_items), so anything at order grain must be de-duplicated: order_count is COUNT(DISTINCT o.order_id), active_customers is COUNT(DISTINCT o.customer_id), and avg_order_value is SUM(line revenue) / NULLIF(COUNT(DISTINCT order_id), 0) to avoid division by zero. Revenue and units are naturally line-level sums. The same fan-out logic appears in insight._additive: order_count is treated as non-additive when grouped by product, category or supplier, because one order can contain several products, so summing per-category order counts would overcount; rates, averages and distinct customer counts are never summed.
questions.reasoning: Fan-out and additivity are core analytics-engineering concepts; this question separates SQL users from modelers.
follow_ups: Why is a sum of distinct counts across months still wrong for active customers?
How would you model a metric at order grain without DISTINCT?

questions.question: Why does the compiler use half-open date ranges with CAST(... AS DATE) literals?
questions.answer: TimeRange has an inclusive start and exclusive end, and its validator rejects end <= start. The compiler emits time_column >= CAST('start' AS DATE) AND time_column < CAST('end' AS DATE). Half-open ranges compose without gaps or overlaps (Q3 ends exactly where Q4 starts), work the same if the column becomes a timestamp, and avoid BETWEEN's inclusive end. Comparing the raw column to a constant keeps the predicate sargable, so the date indexes can be used.
questions.reasoning: Basic but important correctness detail; BETWEEN with timestamps is a classic bug.
follow_ups: Why do the expected-value scripts deliberately use BETWEEN instead?
What breaks if the time column were timestamptz?

questions.question: What does the 77-case evaluation dataset contain?
questions.answer: evaluation/datawise_eval.jsonl is generated by build_expected.py: 36 answered cases with numeric checks, 12 paraphrase_holdout cases that reuse an answered case's check with reworded questions, 10 clarification cases, 12 unsafe cases expecting rejected (DML/DDL intent, users and passwords, pg_catalog, prompt injection, raw SQL, comment markers, tautology) and 7 edge cases (out-of-range period with 0 rows, HAVING threshold row count, two dimensions, the 'mobile' collision, '&' vs 'and' with upper case, last 30 days, an unknown long question). Check types are scalar, top, series and row_count.
questions.reasoning: Baseline knowledge of the eval; interviewers check whether the candidate knows the safety cases are part of it.
follow_ups: Which category would you grow first?
Why include cases that expect clarification?

questions.question: How are expected values kept independent of the system under test?
questions.answer: build_expected.py computes expected numbers with hand-written SQL on the ADMIN connection and never calls the API. The SQL is deliberately phrased differently from the compiler: EXTRACT and BETWEEN instead of DATE_TRUNC and half-open ranges, CASE WHEN on_time THEN 1.0 instead of AVG(CAST(...)), subqueries instead of joins, '!=' instead of '<>'. If both used the same SQL, a definition bug would produce matching wrong numbers. Because the seed is fixed, the values are reproducible and a fresh volume produced identical results.
questions.reasoning: The key concept is an independent oracle; same-code expectations are a common eval anti-pattern.
follow_ups: Is the oracle fully independent? Who decided that cancelled orders are excluded in both?
How would you build an oracle for a real warehouse?

questions.question: Challenge: why do the eval categories authored alongside the planner overstate accuracy?
questions.answer: The answered, clarification, unsafe and edge cases were written by the same author who wrote the rule-based planner, so their phrasing matches the synonyms and cue words the rules know. Their 100% measures that the pipeline -- compiler, joins, filters, time math, insight numbers and safety -- is correct on supported phrasings, not that the system understands language. The held-out paraphrases, written after the planner and intentionally not used for tuning, scored 6/12, which is the honest generalization number. The sample is also small, and the checks are partial (a 'top' check only inspects the first row), so 92.2% overall would be misleading as a headline.
questions.reasoning: This is exactly the eval-literacy question interviewers use to separate practitioners from demo builders.
follow_ups: How would you get a less biased test set cheaply?
Should the failing holdout cases be fixed now? What happens to the holdout if you do?

questions.question: What were the held-out paraphrase failures, and why are they called 'safe failures'?
questions.answer: Six of twelve failed: 'best converting traffic source last year' answered without the traffic-source breakdown because no cue word preceded it; 'how reliable were our vendors in 2026', 'biggest spending customers in 2025', 'total takings for the third quarter of 2025', 'avg order size during 2025' and 'how many days does delivery take on average in 2025' all returned needs_clarification because a word (reliable, spending, takings, the 'avg' variant, the phrasing) was not a known synonym. None returned a wrong number presented as correct. They were deliberately left unfixed so the holdout stays meaningful, and they motivate the LLM planner path.
questions.reasoning: Interviewers want to hear failure analysis by category, plus the discipline of not tuning on the test set.
follow_ups: Is a missing breakdown really 'safe'? What could a user conclude from it?
How would you rank these failures by business impact?

questions.question: How does run_eval.py score an answer, and what are its blind spots?
questions.answer: It logs in, posts each question to /questions/ask, retries 429s with backoff, and calls check_case: the status must match the expected status; then scalar compares the first row's column within a tolerance, top compares the first row's dimension name and value, series compares the full dimension-to-value map, and row_count compares the row count. Blind spots: top checks only the first row, so a wrong limit or ordering after row one passes; insight text and the SQL are not checked; a rejected status passes regardless of which layer rejected it; and clarification cases do not check whether the options are useful. It writes per-case results and p50/p95 to evaluation/results/latest.json.
questions.reasoning: Good evaluators know what their metric does NOT measure.
follow_ups: How would you score clarification quality?
Would you add insight-text checks? How, without being brittle?

questions.question: What do the reported latencies (p50 19 ms, p95 52 ms) actually measure?
questions.answer: They are the server-side latency_ms field from each AskResponse, recorded by run_eval and summarized in evaluation/results/latest.json. AskService measures it with perf_counter from the start of ask() until the response is built, which covers guardrails, planning, compilation, validation, execution and insight, but it is set before _persist, so the history and audit write is excluded, as are auth, middleware and network. The run was sequential with one client against the Docker stack and the local planner, so these are not load-test numbers; latency under concurrency was explicitly not evaluated.
questions.reasoning: Checks that the candidate does not over-claim performance from a single-client run.
follow_ups: What would you expect p95 to look like with an LLM planner?
How would you design a load test for this endpoint?

questions.question: What does the backend test suite cover, and why does it use a real Postgres instead of mocks?
questions.answer: 148 tests pass: validator (45 malicious and safe SQL cases), planner (40 including clarifications and guardrails), timeparse (17), API (15: auth, ask statuses, tenant isolation, reports, catalog, rate limit, request id), compiler (13), executor (12, against the real reader role) and insight (6, compared with independent SQL). conftest.py runs Alembic migrations and both seed scripts at session start, so the suite works on an empty database in CI. A real database is essential because the security claims -- the role cannot write, cannot connect to the app DB, times out -- are properties of Postgres configuration that mocks cannot prove.
questions.reasoning: Interviewers like the argument that security properties of infrastructure must be tested against infrastructure.
follow_ups: What is the downside of DB-backed tests and how do you keep them fast (5.98 s here)?
Which test would you write first for a new metric?

questions.question: How is the eval wired into CI, and how would you improve the gate?
questions.answer: The workspace-level datawise-ci workflow (written, never executed on GitHub) starts Postgres as a service, runs the same db/init script, then ruff, mypy, pytest and pip-audit, starts uvicorn, runs build_expected.py and run_eval.py with --min-accuracy 0.90, and uploads latest.json as an artifact. main() exits 1 when overall accuracy is below the threshold. A single overall threshold is weak: a regression from 12/12 to 11/12 unsafe would still pass at 0.90. I would gate per category (unsafe and clarification must be 100%, answered must not drop versus baseline) and report holdout separately as a tracked, non-blocking metric.
questions.reasoning: Evaluation as a release gate; the per-category point is what interviewers look for.
follow_ups: How do you avoid flaky gates when the planner becomes an LLM?
Should the eval run on every PR or nightly?

questions.question: What observability does the system have today?
questions.answer: structlog emits JSON to stdout with ISO timestamps and log levels, and the request id is bound via contextvars. The middleware logs http_request with method, path, status and duration_ms; AskService logs question_processed with query id, status, provider, latency, row count and org id, never the prompt or secrets. query_history stores status, plan, SQL, provider, latency and error detail per question, and audit_events records logins, failed logins, questions and report changes with request ids. /healthz is liveness and /readyz checks both databases and returns 503 if either is down. There are no metrics endpoint or tracing.
questions.reasoning: Checks that the candidate distinguishes logs, audit trail, health checks and metrics.
follow_ups: What would you add first: metrics or tracing?
Why not log the question text in application logs?

questions.question: How do the insight tests prove that numbers are not fabricated?
questions.answer: test_insight.py calls the real API and compares the returned values with direct SQL on the admin connection: total revenue 2025, top product, conversion rate and on-time rate by supplier. test_time_series_change_is_computed_from_rows checks the percent change is derived from rows, and test_empty_result_has_honest_insight asks for 2023 (outside the data window) and expects 'No data matched' instead of an invented value. On top of that, build_insight first runs verify(), which checks result columns match the plan and metric values are numeric, and returns no insight if they do not.
questions.reasoning: Probes testing of grounded generation, including the empty-data case most systems get wrong.
follow_ups: How would you test an LLM-generated narrative for faithfulness?
What insight bug would these tests not catch?

questions.question: Design the production monitoring for this system. What would you alert on?
questions.answer: Not implemented beyond logs and tables. From query_history and logs I would chart status mix (answered / clarification / rejected / error) per org and provider, p50/p95 latency per stage (planner, execution), query_timeout and analytics_unavailable rates, and LLM cost per question once usage is persisted. Alerts: any validator rejection of compiled SQL (should be zero, so it indicates a compiler bug or tampering), any read_only_violation, a spike in guardrail rejections (probing), and a jump in clarification rate after a deploy. I would also mine clarification questions' unmapped words to build a synonym backlog, and add thumbs up/down feedback to measure answer usefulness, which the eval cannot.
questions.reasoning: Senior observability design: signals tied to the system's invariants, not generic CPU dashboards.
follow_ups: How do you avoid alert fatigue from guardrail false positives?
Which metric would tell you the planner is drifting?

questions.question: How does authentication work?
questions.answer: Passwords are hashed with argon2 via argon2-cffi's PasswordHasher. POST /auth/login looks up the user by lower-cased email, verifies the hash and returns an HS256 JWT with sub (user id), org, role, iat and exp (60 minutes by default). get_current_user requires a Bearer token, decodes it requiring exp and sub, loads the user and rejects the token if the user no longer exists or the org claim does not match the user's current org. The frontend stores the token in localStorage and clears it on any 401.
questions.reasoning: Standard auth check; the org-claim match against the DB is the detail that shows care.
follow_ups: Why check the org claim against the database instead of trusting the token?
How would you revoke a token before it expires?

questions.question: How is tenant isolation enforced for history and saved reports, and why return 404 instead of 403?
questions.answer: Every app-DB row carries org_id. The history endpoint filters QueryHistory by user.org_id; report endpoints load through _get_owned, which returns 404 'Report not found' if the report does not exist or belongs to another org. A 403 would confirm that the id exists, letting an attacker enumerate other tenants' report ids. test_history_is_tenant_isolated and test_saved_reports_crud_rerun_and_isolation use two orgs (Acme and Globex) and assert that Globex cannot see, run, rename or delete Acme's report.
questions.reasoning: Classic multi-tenancy question; the 404-vs-403 reasoning is a standard follow-up.
follow_ups: Where would a forgotten org filter most likely slip in?
Would Postgres RLS on the app DB be worth it here?

questions.question: Challenge: the analytics data is shared across orgs. Is that a security bug?
questions.answer: In this demo it is a documented limitation, not a bug: there is one synthetic company, so Acme and Globex users see the same business data while their history, reports and audit are isolated by org_id. The threat model lists it as a residual risk and says a real multi-tenant deployment needs per-tenant analytics databases or row-level security keyed on the org. It would become a bug the moment real tenant data is loaded, and it also affects the value index, which loads customer and product names for the planner from the whole analytics DB. I would be explicit about this in a design review rather than let 'org isolation' in the README imply more than it covers.
questions.reasoning: Tests precision in security claims: knowing exactly what is and is not isolated.
follow_ups: Which is better for B2B analytics: database per tenant or RLS?
How would the value index work per tenant?

questions.question: Design row-level security per tenant on the analytics database.
questions.answer: Not implemented. Add a tenant_id column to every analytics table, enable RLS with FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY and a policy USING (tenant_id = current_setting('app.tenant_id')::int), and make sure datawise_reader is neither the table owner nor BYPASSRLS. execute_readonly would run SET LOCAL app.tenant_id inside the same transaction before the query; this is executor code, not validated SQL, so it does not conflict with the validator blocking Set nodes and set_config. As a second layer, the compiler could add tenant_id to each Fact's base_where. The value index and catalog caches must become per tenant, or customer names leak through planner suggestions. Tests: a cross-tenant query as the reader must return only own rows even with the predicate removed.
questions.reasoning: System-design question with a sharp edge: cache leakage and session-variable handling.
follow_ups: What happens with connection pooling if SET (not SET LOCAL) is used?
How do indexes change once every query filters by tenant_id?

questions.question: How do the guardrails handle prompt injection, and why are they not the real defense?
questions.answer: check_question runs four regex rules before any planner: prompt_injection ('ignore ... instructions', 'system prompt', 'you are now', 'developer mode', 'act as', 'bypass'), raw_sql (semicolons, comment markers, UNION SELECT, '1=1', pg_sleep, dblink), write_intent (delete, drop, update, grant and similar) and sensitive_data (passwords, tokens, pg_*, information_schema, user lists). A hit returns rejected with the category in validation issues, and it is persisted and audited. They are a UX and cost layer: they stop obvious abuse before paying for LLM tokens. The real guarantees come later -- even an injection that fools a model can only produce a QueryPlan validated against the semantic layer, compiled by our code and run read-only.
questions.reasoning: Interviewers want to hear 'guardrails reduce noise, structure provides safety'.
follow_ups: Give an injection phrasing these regexes miss.
What is the cost of a guardrail false positive here?

questions.question: What is the risk of storing the JWT in localStorage, and how would you harden it?
questions.answer: Any XSS can read localStorage and exfiltrate the token, which is valid for 60 minutes with no revocation. Mitigations present: React escapes rendered data (the SPA never renders HTML from query results), and nginx sets X-Content-Type-Options, X-Frame-Options DENY and a Referrer-Policy. Missing: a Content-Security-Policy, refresh tokens, revocation and lockout. The documented hardening step is an httpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookie with CSRF protection, which removes token access from JavaScript; with a cookie you also need CSRF tokens or strict SameSite for the POST endpoints.
questions.reasoning: Standard web-security trade-off; good answers mention CSP and CSRF together.
follow_ups: Is a short-lived token in memory plus a refresh cookie better?
What CSP would this SPA need, given Recharts and Tailwind?

questions.question: How are failed logins handled, and is user enumeration really prevented?
questions.answer: login returns the same 401 'Invalid email or password' for an unknown email and a wrong password, and records an auth.login_failed audit event (org and user are null when the email is unknown). Originally, verify_password was skipped for unknown users, so the response was measurably faster than for an existing user, because argon2 is deliberately slow; that timing difference could enumerate accounts. It was fixed by verifying against a module-level dummy hash (_DUMMY_HASH) when the user is missing, so both paths pay the same cost. There is still no lockout and no per-IP limit on login; the ask rate limiter does not cover it.
questions.reasoning: Detail-oriented security question; spotting and explaining the timing side channel is a strong signal.
follow_ups: How would you rate-limit login without enabling lockout-based denial of service?
Should failed-login audit events store the attempted email?

questions.question: How does the system defend against a tampered saved-report plan?
questions.answer: Threat T11. On create, SavedReportCreate.plan is parsed as a QueryPlan (extra='forbid', typed filters) and compile_plan must succeed, otherwise 422 invalid_plan (test_saved_report_rejects_invalid_plan posts metrics=['passwords']). On every run, run_report loads the stored JSON through QueryPlan.model_validate again and calls run_plan, which recompiles and re-validates the SQL before the read-only executor. So even if someone edits the JSON column directly in the app DB, the worst case is a plan that fails validation or produces an allowlisted query. There is no SQL stored to tamper with.
questions.reasoning: Tests the principle of re-validating data at use time, not only at write time.
follow_ups: What if a plan is valid but a metric it references is later removed?
Would you sign stored plans?

questions.question: Why is the local planner so fast, and what does a question cost?
questions.answer: LocalPlanner does no network calls: it lower-cases and normalizes the text, runs parse_time, and scans precompiled regexes for every metric synonym, dimension synonym and known dimension value, then applies rules. Its Usage is all zeros, so the marginal cost is CPU only. Server-side latency in the eval was p50 19 ms and p95 52 ms, which includes the SQL execution on a small synthetic dataset. An LLM planner would add a network round trip and per-token cost to every question, and up to double with a repair retry.
questions.reasoning: Simple, but interviewers want numbers from the actual results file, not guesses.
follow_ups: Does the regex scan scale with the number of products and customers? How?
Where would you cache to make it even cheaper?

questions.question: The executor opens a new psycopg connection per question. What are the implications?
questions.answer: execute_readonly calls psycopg.connect for every query, which costs a TCP handshake, authentication and backend process startup on each request -- fine at demo load and very simple to reason about, since the connection is discarded after the rollback. Under load it adds latency and can exhaust max_connections. A psycopg_pool ConnectionPool for the reader would fix that, and it is safe here because both SET TRANSACTION READ ONLY and SET LOCAL statement_timeout are transaction-scoped and the executor always rolls back, so no session state leaks between requests.
questions.reasoning: Probes pooling knowledge and whether the candidate checks that session state is safe to pool.
follow_ups: Which session-level settings would make pooling dangerous?
Would PgBouncer transaction pooling work here?

questions.question: Design result caching keyed by a normalized plan.
questions.answer: Not implemented (roadmap item 6 suggests caching keyed on compiled SQL). Plans are a good key because relative dates are already resolved to absolute start/end dates before compilation. I would key on a hash of the canonical plan JSON (sorted keys, assumptions removed, IN lists sorted) or the compiled SQL, plus the semantic-layer version, a data version (ETL watermark), and the tenant once analytics is multi-tenant. Store columns, rows and truncated in Redis with a TTL, cache only successful executions, and still run build_insight and write history on hits so auditing stays complete. Invalidation on data load is the hard part, which is why the data version belongs in the key rather than relying on deletes.
questions.reasoning: Caching design with correct invalidation thinking; the 'resolved dates' observation is a strong detail.
follow_ups: Why not cache by question text?
How would you prevent a thundering herd on a popular report?

questions.question: What drives the cost of an LLM-planned question, and how would you control it?
questions.answer: Input tokens are dominated by the system prompt, which includes describe_for_prompt() -- every metric, synonyms and dimension -- and grows with the semantic layer; output is a small JSON plan. A repair retry roughly doubles the cost, and estimate_cost reports an estimate from PRICES_PER_MTOK. Controls: reject unsafe questions with guardrails before calling the model (already done), answer with the local planner first and only fall back to the LLM (hybrid, proposed), use provider prompt caching for the static system prompt, cache plans per normalized question, and alert on repair rates. No live cost has been measured because the providers were never run.
questions.reasoning: Cost reasoning without invented numbers; mentioning that guardrails save tokens is a nice touch.
follow_ups: How would you trim the prompt as the semantic layer grows to 200 metrics?
When is caching plans by question text safe?

questions.question: Where are the bounds on result size and memory, and what precision trade-off is made?
questions.answer: Results are bounded three times: the compiler clamps LIMIT to MAX_ROWS (1000), the validator rejects any LIMIT above it, and the executor uses fetchmany(max_rows + 1) so even unbounded SQL cannot flood memory and truncation is detected and mentioned in the insight. _jsonable converts Decimal to float and dates to ISO strings for JSON; metric SQL rounds currency to 2 decimals and rates to 4, so float is acceptable for display, but it is not exact for accounting-grade totals. On the client, the table renders up to 1000 rows and toChartData caps series at 8.
questions.reasoning: Tests layered limits and awareness of Decimal-to-float precision loss.
follow_ups: When would you send decimals as strings instead?
Is 1000 rows the right cap for a chart?

questions.question: How would you scale the analytics side to hundreds of millions of order lines?
questions.answer: Not implemented. First, move analytics to a read replica or a columnar warehouse, which deployment.md already anticipates via ANALYTICS_READER_DATABASE_URL. Second, partition the fact tables by date and add rollup tables or materialized views per fact and grain (day x product, month x region).
